summary: According to the closing note of Greek Esther, Dositheus 'who said he was a priest and Levite' and his son Ptolemeus brought the Letter of Purim (the Greek Esther) to Egypt in the fourth year of Ptolemy and Cleopatra; it had been translated in Jerusalem by Lysimachus son of Ptolemeus.
catholic: This colophon (Est 10:14 in this text) is a rare ancient note about how a biblical book was translated and transmitted.
know: Named in the colophon of Greek Esther.

name: Elisheba
summary: Daughter of Amminadab of Judah and sister of Nahshon, prince of Judah. She married Aaron and bore Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, so that the priestly line of Israel descends from her.
catholic: Elisheba unites the priestly tribe of Levi with the royal tribe of Judah. Some Christian writers note that her name is the Hebrew form of 'Elizabeth', borne by the priestly mother of John the Baptist, who was 'of the daughters of Aaron' (Lk 1:5).
know: Daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon (Exo 6:23).
Wife of Aaron.
Mother of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.

name: Eunice
summary: Eunice was a Jewish woman who became a believer, the wife of a Greek, and the mother of Timothy. Paul praises the 'sincere faith' that lived in her and in her mother Lois before it lived in Timothy.
catholic: With Lois she is a model of mothers and grandmothers who hand on the faith, the family as 'domestic church' where children first learn the Scriptures (2 Tim 3:15).
know: A believing Jewish woman married to a Greek (Acts 16:1).
Mother of Timothy (2 Tim 1:5).

name: Euodia
summary: Euodia was one of two women at Philippi who had laboured with Paul in the gospel; Paul urges her and Syntyche to 'think the same way in the Lord' and asks a 'true partner' to help them reconcile.
catholic: Paul's appeal is a model of fraternal reconciliation within the Church; he honors both women as co-workers whose names are in the book of life.
know: Laboured with Paul in the gospel (Phil 4:3).
Urged to agree with her fellow worker (Phil 4:2).

name: Eutychus
summary: Eutychus was a young man at Troas who fell asleep in a window during Paul's long sermon on the first day of the week and fell three stories to his death. Paul went down, embraced him, and he was restored to life; the gathering then broke bread and continued till dawn.
catholic: The setting, the community gathered 'on the first day of the week... to break bread' (Acts 20:7), is an early witness to the Sunday Eucharist (cf. CCC 1343).
know: Fell from a third-story window at Troas.
Raised by Paul (Acts 20:10-12).
The scene takes place at a Sunday breaking of bread (Acts 20:7).

name: Gaius (of 3 John)
summary: Gaius 'the beloved' is the addressee of the Third Letter of John. The Elder praises him for walking in the truth and for his faithful hospitality to travelling missionaries, in contrast to Diotrephes.
catholic: Gaius is a model of Christian hospitality to those who go out 'for the sake of the Name' (3 John 7), making him a 'fellow worker for the truth'.
know: Addressee of 3 John.
Praised for welcoming travelling brothers (3 John 5-8).

name: Gomer
summary: Gomer, daughter of Diblaim, was the wife God told Hosea to marry, 'a wife of prostitution'. She bore three children whose names announced judgment on Israel; her unfaithfulness and Hosea's command to love her again mirror Israel's idolatry and God's faithful love.
catholic: In the Church's reading Gomer stands for Israel — and every soul — unfaithful to God, whom the divine Bridegroom pursues and restores; the pattern is fulfilled in Christ who loves the Church and gives himself up for her (Eph 5:25).
know: Daughter of Diblaim (Hos 1:3).
Mother of Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi.
Hos 3:1-3 (Hosea buys back an adulterous woman) is usually understood to refer to Gomer.

name: Heli
summary: Heli is named in Luke's genealogy as the father of Joseph, 'the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli' (Lk 3:23).
catholic: Matthew names Joseph's father as Jacob (Mt 1:16). Ancient and modern interpreters reconcile the two: Julius Africanus (3rd century) proposed a levirate marriage, making one the natural and the other the legal father, while others hold that Luke traces Mary's line, Heli being Joseph's father-in-law. The Church has not defined the question.
know: Named only in Luke 3:23.
Matthew 1:16 names Jacob as Joseph's father - the two genealogies differ here.
Some interpreters read Luke's line as Mary's, making Heli her father; Tradition otherwise names her father Joachim.

name: Jason of Cyrene
summary: The Jewish historian whose five-volume history of the Maccabean revolt the author of 2 Maccabees abridged into one book.
catholic: The epitomist's preface and epilogue (2 Macc 2:19-32; 15:37-39), describing the toil of condensing a source, are a candid witness that inspired authors used human sources and labor — a point the Church notes in teaching that God used human authors 'with their own faculties and powers' (cf. CCC 106).
know: Wrote five books on the revolt (2 Macc 2:23).

name: Jesus son of Sirach
summary: Jesus (Yeshua) son of Eleazar son of Sirach, a scribe and teacher of wisdom in Jerusalem around 190-180 BC, wrote the book of Sirach, whose Greek translation was made by his grandson in Egypt. His book unites wisdom with the Law and Temple worship and closes with the great 'praise of the fathers' (Sir 44-50), from Enoch to the high priest Simon son of Onias.
catholic: Sirach is a deuterocanonical book, received in the Church's canon (Rome 382, Carthage 397, Trent 1546). Its Latin name Ecclesiasticus ('the Church's book') reflects its constant use in teaching catechumens and the faithful, and it is read often in the Lectionary. Its portrait of Wisdom dwelling in Israel (Sir 24) prepares for John's prologue ('the Word became flesh and dwelt among us'), and its 'praise of the fathers' is a model for Hebrews 11.
know: Signs his book in Sir 50:27.
Book also called Ecclesiasticus.
His grandson's translator's prologue is not versified in this text.
The 'praise of the fathers' omits Ezra but includes Nehemiah (Sir 49:13).

name: Jezebel of Thyatira
summary: In the letter to Thyatira the risen Christ rebukes the church for tolerating 'that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess' and leads his servants into immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols; she was given time to repent but refused.
catholic: Whether a real woman or a symbolic name, she is called after Ahab's queen Jezebel, who led Israel into idolatry; she stands for false teaching that compromises with pagan practice.
know: Named in Rev 2:20.
Called by the name of the idolatrous queen Jezebel (1 Kings 16-21).
Given time to repent but refused (Rev 2:21).

name: Joseph Barsabbas
summary: Joseph called Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, was one of the two disciples proposed to replace Judas Iscariot among the Twelve; the lot fell on Matthias instead.
catholic: He is honored as one of the early disciples who had followed Jesus throughout his public ministry. His candidacy shows the criterion of apostolic witness to the whole ministry of Jesus.
know: Also called Justus (Acts 1:23).
A witness of Jesus' whole ministry, from John's baptism to the Ascension.
Not chosen: the lot fell on Matthias.

name: Junia
summary: Junia, with Andronicus, was a relative and fellow prisoner of Paul, 'notable among the apostles', and in Christ before Paul.
catholic: St John Chrysostom praised her as a woman worthy to be called 'among the apostles'. With Andronicus, commonly thought to be her husband, she is honored as a saint; 'apostles' here is generally understood in the wider sense of missionaries.
know: Greeted with Andronicus in Rom 16:7.
Called 'notable among the apostles'.
A believer before Paul.

name: King Lemuel
summary: An otherwise unknown king to whom Proverbs 31 is attributed, recording 'the revelation which his mother taught him' — advice against wine and women's wiles, a charge to defend the poor, and (probably) the poem of the capable wife.
catholic: The poem of the 'worthy woman' (Prov 31:10-31) that closes Proverbs is read in the Church as a portrait of holy womanhood and has been applied to the Church and to Mary; it is read in the Lectionary (e.g. 33rd Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year A).
know: Author of Proverbs 31 (at least 31:1-9).
Taught by his mother (Prov 31:1).

name: Linus
summary: Linus is one of the Roman Christians who send greetings to Timothy in Paul's final letter.
catholic: St Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.3) records that the apostles Peter and Paul entrusted the office of bishop of Rome to Linus, 'of whom Paul makes mention in the Epistles to Timothy'. He is therefore honored as St Linus, the first successor of St Peter as Pope; he is named in the Roman Canon ('Linus, Cletus, Clement') and commemorated on September 23. His place at the head of the list of Roman bishops is a classic witness to apostolic succession.
know: Greets Timothy in 2 Tim 4:21.
Identified by St Irenaeus as Peter's first successor as bishop of Rome.
Named in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I).

name: Lo-ammi
summary: Gomer's second son, named Lo-ammi ('not my people') as a sign of the broken covenant; God promises that those called 'not my people' will be called 'sons of the living God'.
catholic: St Paul (Rom 9:25-26) and St Peter (1 Pet 2:10) see the reversal 'not my people... my people' fulfilled in the Church, gathered from Jews and Gentiles.
know: Name means 'not my people'.
Reversed in Hos 1:10 and 2:23; quoted in Rom 9:25-26.

name: Lois
summary: Lois was Timothy's grandmother, in whom, Paul writes, a sincere faith 'lived first' before passing to Timothy's mother Eunice and to Timothy himself.
catholic: Honored as an example of grandparents who transmit the faith across generations.
know: Timothy's grandmother (2 Tim 1:5).
Often assumed to be Eunice's mother, though the text does not say whether she was Timothy's maternal or paternal grandmother.

name: Malachi
summary: Malachi ('my messenger') prophesied in the 5th century BC to a discouraged post-exilic community, rebuking priests who offered blemished sacrifices, men who divorced the wives of their youth, and people who robbed God of tithes. He announced that the Lord would send his messenger to prepare the way and would send Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible Day of the LORD.
catholic: Malachi 1:11 — 'in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering' — is taught by the Council of Trent (Session XXII, ch. 1) to be fulfilled in the Sacrifice of the Mass, offered among all nations, and is echoed in Eucharistic Prayer III ('from the rising of the sun to its setting'). Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the messenger of Mal 3:1 and as the Elijah who was to come (Mt 11:10, 14; cf. Lk 1:17). Mal 3:1-4, the Lord coming suddenly to his Temple, is read on the feast of the Presentation (February 2).
know: Last book of the Old Testament in the Christian canon.
'A pure offering' among the nations (Mal 1:11) — the Mass.
'I send my messenger to prepare the way before me' (Mal 3:1).
Promise of Elijah's return (Mal 4:5-6), fulfilled in John the Baptist.

name: Malchus
summary: Malchus was the servant of the high priest whose right ear Simon Peter cut off with a sword at Jesus' arrest. Jesus ordered Peter to put away the sword, and Luke records that he touched the ear and healed it.
catholic: The scene shows Christ freely accepting his Passion ('the cup which the Father has given me') and healing even an enemy, his last miracle before the cross.
know: Servant of the high priest (Jn 18:10).
His ear was cut off by Peter (Jn 18:10).
Healed by Jesus (Lk 22:51).

name: Manaen
summary: Manaen, 'the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch', was among the prophets and teachers at Antioch who commissioned Barnabas and Saul.
catholic: His presence shows the Gospel reaching even the court of Herod Antipas, who beheaded John the Baptist.
know: Raised with Herod Antipas (Acts 13:1).
A leader of the church at Antioch.

name: Mary, mother of John Mark
summary: Mary was the mother of John Mark. Her house in Jerusalem was a gathering place where many were praying for Peter during his imprisonment, and Peter went there first after his miraculous release.
catholic: She is an early example of a house church, the domestic setting where the first Christians gathered for prayer. Some later tradition identifies her house with the place of the Last Supper, but Scripture does not say so.
know: Mother of John Mark.
Many gathered to pray in her house during Peter's imprisonment.
Rhoda was a servant in her house.

name: Mattatha
summary: Mattatha, son of Nathan son of David, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs from Joseph back through David's son Nathan to Adam; he is listed as the father of Menan (Lk 3:31).
catholic: Luke traces Jesus' ancestry back to Adam, 'the son of God' (Lk 3:38), showing him as Saviour of the whole human race; unlike Matthew, his line descends through David's son Nathan rather than Solomon.
know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:31).
Son of Nathan son of David; father of Menan.

name: Medium of Endor
summary: On the eve of his last battle Saul, in disguise, asked a woman at Endor who had a familiar spirit to bring up Samuel; Samuel appeared and foretold Saul's death and Israel's defeat.
catholic: Saul's visit breaks the law he himself had enforced against mediums (1 Sam 28:3; Deut 18:10-12). The Church teaches that all recourse to mediums and conjuring the dead must be rejected (CCC 2116). Sirach 46:20 says Samuel prophesied after his death.
know: Saul had earlier banished mediums
Samuel's spirit foretold Saul's death
Fed Saul before he left

name: Moab
summary: Son of Lot by his elder daughter, born after the destruction of Sodom; ancestor of the Moabites.
catholic: Through the Moabite Ruth, a descendant of Lot's line enters the ancestry of David and of Christ (Mt 1:5).
know: Ancestor of the Moabites (Gen 19:37)
Ruth the Moabitess descends from his people

name: Nahum
summary: Nahum the Elkoshite announced the fall of Nineveh, the cruel Assyrian capital, which happened in 612 BC. His poem celebrates God as slow to anger but great in power, a refuge for those who trust him and a judge of oppressors.
catholic: Nahum 1:15 ('on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace') is echoed in Isaiah 52:7 and applied by St Paul to the preachers of the Gospel (Rom 10:15).
know: From Elkosh (location unknown).
Prophesied the fall of Nineveh (612 BC).
Contrast with Jonah, where Nineveh repents.

name: Neri
summary: Neri, son of Melchi, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs from Joseph back through David's son Nathan to Adam; he is listed as the father of Shealtiel (Lk 3:27).
catholic: Luke traces Jesus' ancestry back to Adam, 'the son of God' (Lk 3:38), showing him as Saviour of the whole human race; unlike Matthew, his line descends through David's son Nathan rather than Solomon.
know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:27).
Son of Melchi; father of Shealtiel.
Luke makes him Shealtiel's father, whereas Matthew 1:12 and 1 Chronicles 3:17 give Jechoniah.

name: Nicanor
summary: Nicanor was one of the Seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen by the Jerusalem church to serve at table so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.
catholic: The choice of the Seven, on whom the apostles laid hands after prayer (Acts 6:6), is traditionally read as the institution of the diaconate, the first degree of Holy Orders, ordained 'not unto the priesthood but unto the ministry' (CCC 1569-1571).
know: Named among the Seven in Acts 6:5.
Received the laying on of hands from the apostles (Acts 6:6).

name: Nicolaus
summary: Nicolaus, 'a proselyte of Antioch', was the last named of the Seven chosen to serve the Jerusalem church; as a convert to Judaism from paganism he shows the early Church already drawing in Gentile-born believers.
catholic: The choice of the Seven, on whom the apostles laid hands after prayer (Acts 6:6), is traditionally read as the institution of the diaconate, the first degree of Holy Orders, ordained 'not unto the priesthood but unto the ministry' (CCC 1569-1571). Some early writers (e.g. St Irenaeus) connected the Nicolaitans of Revelation 2 with him, but this is uncertain and other Fathers defended his memory.
know: The only one of the Seven whose origin is given: a proselyte of Antioch.
Received the laying on of hands (Acts 6:6).
Any link with the Nicolaitans (Rev 2:6, 2:15) is a later and disputed tradition.

name: Obadiah
summary: Obadiah is the author of the shortest book of the Old Testament, a single vision against Edom for gloating over and plundering Jerusalem on the day of its fall, ending with the promise that 'the kingdom will be the LORD's'.
catholic: Obadiah teaches that God judges pride and cruelty toward a brother nation (Edom descended from Esau, Israel from Jacob) and that the final kingdom belongs to God, fulfilled in the Kingdom Christ inaugurates.
know: Shortest book of the Old Testament (21 verses).
Not the Obadiah of Ahab's household in 1 Kings 18.
Usually dated after Jerusalem's fall in 587 BC.

name: Parmenas
summary: Parmenas was one of the Seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen by the Jerusalem church to serve at table so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.
catholic: The choice of the Seven, on whom the apostles laid hands after prayer (Acts 6:6), is traditionally read as the institution of the diaconate, the first degree of Holy Orders, ordained 'not unto the priesthood but unto the ministry' (CCC 1569-1571).
know: Named among the Seven in Acts 6:5.
Received the laying on of hands from the apostles (Acts 6:6).

name: Philemon
summary: Philemon was a beloved fellow worker of Paul, in whose house a church met, and the master of the slave Onesimus. Paul's shortest letter asks him to welcome Onesimus back as a brother in Christ.
catholic: Philemon is a model of the house church and of the charity that must reshape relationships between Christians; Paul appeals 'for love's sake' rather than commanding (Philem 8-9). See CCC 2414 on Onesimus.
know: Addressee of the Letter to Philemon.
A church met in his house (Philem 2).
Paul says Philemon owes him 'even your own self' (Philem 19), implying Paul converted him.
Apphia and Archippus are greeted with him; they are often thought to be his wife and son, but the letter does not say so.

name: Phoebe
role: Minister of the church at Cenchreae
summary: Phoebe, 'our sister', was a servant (Greek diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae, the port of Corinth. Paul commends her to the Romans, who are to welcome her and help her, for she had been a patron of many, including Paul; she is generally thought to have carried the Letter to the Romans.
catholic: She is honored as a saint. Her title diakonos ('servant, minister') shows that women held recognized ministries of service in the apostolic Church; the precise nature of her role is discussed by scholars, and the Church distinguishes later deaconesses from the ordained diaconate.
know: From Cenchreae near Corinth (Rom 16:1).
Called diakonos, 'servant' or 'minister', of the church.
A 'helper' (patron) of many and of Paul (Rom 16:2).

name: Prochorus
summary: Prochorus was one of the Seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen by the Jerusalem church to serve at table so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.
catholic: The choice of the Seven, on whom the apostles laid hands after prayer (Acts 6:6), is traditionally read as the institution of the diaconate, the first degree of Holy Orders, ordained 'not unto the priesthood but unto the ministry' (CCC 1569-1571).
know: Named among the Seven in Acts 6:5.
Received the laying on of hands from the apostles (Acts 6:6).

name: Puah
summary: The second of the two Hebrew midwives who feared God and refused Pharaoh's order to kill the Hebrew baby boys.
catholic: With Shiphrah, Puah is held up as a witness to the dignity of human life and to obeying God rather than an unjust law.
know: Hebrew midwife in Egypt (Exo 1:15).
Defied Pharaoh to save newborn boys.
Not the same as Puah, father of the judge Tola.

name: Razis
summary: An elder of Jerusalem called 'Father of the Jews' for his goodwill, whom Nicanor tried to arrest. Rather than fall into the hands of sinners he took his own life in a dramatic manner, calling on the Lord of life to give his body back to him.
catholic: The Church does not hold up Razis' suicide as an example — Catholic moral teaching forbids suicide (CCC 2280-2283) — but the passage is a witness to his faith in bodily resurrection (2 Macc 14:46). St Augustine, answering Donatists who cited Razis, denied that his death was an example to imitate.
know: Called 'Father of the Jews' (2 Macc 14:37).
Died rather than be captured by Nicanor (2 Macc 14:37-46).

name: Rhesa
summary: Rhesa, son of Zerubbabel, appears only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs from Joseph back through David's son Nathan to Adam; he is listed as the father of Joanan (Lk 3:27).
catholic: Luke traces Jesus' ancestry back to Adam, 'the son of God' (Lk 3:38), showing him as Saviour of the whole human race; unlike Matthew, his line descends through David's son Nathan rather than Solomon.
know: Named only in Luke's genealogy (Lk 3:27).
Son of Zerubbabel; father of Joanan.
Luke's line leaves Matthew's at Zerubbabel: Matthew continues through Abiud, Luke through Rhesa.

name: Rhoda
summary: Rhoda was a servant girl in the house of Mary, mother of John Mark. When Peter, freed from prison by an angel, knocked at the gate, she recognized his voice and in her joy ran to tell the others without opening the door.
catholic: A vivid detail of the praying Church in Jerusalem, whose prayer for Peter was answered while they still doubted.
know: Recognized Peter's voice at the gate.
Ran in to announce him before opening, and was not believed at first.

name: Sapphira
summary: Wife of Ananias, she conspired with him to keep back part of the price of their land. Questioned by Peter three hours after her husband's death, she repeated the lie and died at once.
catholic: Her story pairs with her husband's as a sober lesson on honesty before God and the seriousness of sins against the Holy Spirit in the Church.
know: Wife of Ananias, she shared in his deception.
Peter asked her directly the price of the land; she lied.
She died and was buried beside her husband.

name: Sceva
summary: Sceva was a Jewish chief priest whose seven sons, itinerant exorcists, tried to cast out demons 'by Jesus whom Paul preaches'; the evil spirit answered, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?' and overpowered them.
catholic: The episode shows that the name of Jesus is not a magic formula; the Church's exorcisms are acts of faith exercised in the Church's authority.
know: Father of seven sons who were itinerant exorcists (Acts 19:14).
The episode led many in Ephesus to burn their magic books (Acts 19:19).

name: Sergius Paulus
summary: Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus and 'a man of understanding', summoned Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God. When the sorcerer Elymas opposed them and was struck blind, the proconsul believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
catholic: The first Roman official recorded as believing in Acts; it is at this encounter that Saul is first called Paul (Acts 13:9).
know: Proconsul of Cyprus at Paphos.
Believed after Elymas was blinded (Acts 13:12).

name: Shear-jashub
summary: Isaiah's son, who went with his father to meet King Ahaz at the upper pool. His name means 'a remnant will return', a living sign of Isaiah's message.
catholic: His name embodies the prophetic theme of the faithful remnant, which the Church sees fulfilled in those who receive Christ (cf. Rom 9:27, 11:5).
know: Name means 'a remnant shall return'.
Accompanied Isaiah to meet Ahaz (Isa 7:3).
Isaiah says he and his children are 'for signs' in Israel (Isa 8:18).

name: Shiphrah
summary: One of two Hebrew midwives ordered by Pharaoh to kill newborn Hebrew boys. Fearing God, she and Puah let the boys live, and God dealt well with them and gave them households.
catholic: Shiphrah and Puah are often cited in Catholic teaching as early examples of conscientious refusal to take innocent life at the command of the state: they 'feared God' rather than the king (Exo 1:17).
know: Hebrew midwife in Egypt (Exo 1:15).
Refused Pharaoh's order to kill the boys.
God rewarded her with a household (Exo 1:21).

name: Simeon called Niger
summary: Simeon, called Niger ('black'), was one of the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch who, at the Spirit's command, laid hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent them out.
catholic: With the other leaders of Antioch he took part in the prayer, fasting and laying on of hands that commissioned the first missionary journey (Acts 13:3).
know: Listed among the prophets and teachers at Antioch.
Some suggest, without certainty, that he is Simon of Cyrene.

name: Simon II the high priest
summary: Simon son of Onias, high priest around 200 BC, who repaired and fortified the Temple and the city. Sirach ends his 'praise of the fathers' with a glowing portrait of him coming out of the sanctuary in his vestments and offering sacrifice amid the trumpets and the people's prayer, blessing the people in the Lord's name.
catholic: Sirach 50 is one of the most vivid descriptions of Temple liturgy in Scripture; the high priest emerging 'like the morning star' to bless the people has been read as a figure of Christ the High Priest who enters the true sanctuary and blesses his people (Heb 9:11-12; Luke 24:50-51).
know: Praised in Sirach 50:1-21.
Son of Onias (Sir 50:1).
According to Josephus, father of Onias III (not stated in Scripture).

name: Syntyche
summary: Syntyche was one of two women at Philippi who had laboured with Paul in the gospel; Paul urges her and Euodia to 'think the same way in the Lord' and asks a 'true partner' to help them reconcile.
catholic: Paul's appeal is a model of fraternal reconciliation within the Church; he honors both women as co-workers whose names are in the book of life.
know: Laboured with Paul in the gospel (Phil 4:3).
Urged to agree with her fellow worker (Phil 4:2).

name: Tiberius Caesar
summary: Tiberius succeeded Augustus as emperor (AD 14-37). Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to 'the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar' (Lk 3:1), and Jesus' public life, death and resurrection took place under his rule.
catholic: The 'Caesar' whose image was on the denarius when Jesus said 'Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mt 22:21) was Tiberius - a key text for Catholic teaching on the relation of Church and state. Antipas named the city of Tiberias, on the Sea of Tiberias, after him (Jn 6:1).
know: Emperor AD 14-37; adopted son and successor of Augustus.
His fifteenth year dates John's ministry (Lk 3:1).
Reigning emperor during Jesus' ministry and crucifixion.

name: Timon
summary: Timon was one of the Seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen by the Jerusalem church to serve at table so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.
catholic: The choice of the Seven, on whom the apostles laid hands after prayer (Acts 6:6), is traditionally read as the institution of the diaconate, the first degree of Holy Orders, ordained 'not unto the priesthood but unto the ministry' (CCC 1569-1571).
know: Named among the Seven in Acts 6:5.
Received the laying on of hands from the apostles (Acts 6:6).

name: Zephaniah
summary: Zephaniah, son of Cushi and a descendant of a certain Hezekiah, prophesied in the reign of King Josiah. He proclaimed the Day of the LORD as a day of wrath against idolatry in Judah and the nations, promised a humble and lowly remnant, and ended with a joyful song: 'Sing, daughter of Zion... the LORD your God is in the midst of you'.
catholic: The medieval sequence 'Dies irae' takes its opening words from Zephaniah 1:15 in the Latin Vulgate ('dies irae dies illa'). His call 'Sing, daughter of Zion' (Zeph 3:14-17), echoed in Gabriel's 'Rejoice' to Mary, is read in Advent and on the feast of the Visitation, and the Church sees Mary as the Daughter of Zion in whom the Lord dwells. His 'humble and lowly people' (Zeph 3:12) are the 'anawim', the poor of the Lord, whose spirituality Mary embodies in the Magnificat.
know: Genealogy back four generations to a 'Hezekiah' (Zeph 1:1), possibly the king.
Prophesied under Josiah (c. 640-609 BC).
Source of the 'Dies irae' (Zeph 1:15).
'Sing, daughter of Zion!' (Zeph 3:14).

name: Anne
summary: Scripture does not name the Virgin Mary's mother. Tradition, beginning with the Protoevangelium of James, names her Anne, a long-childless wife who with Joachim was granted a daughter, Mary.
catholic: Tradition holds that Anne conceived Mary after years of barrenness and prayer, and the Church celebrates Mary's Immaculate Conception in Anne's womb (December 8) and her Nativity (September 8). St Anne is a beloved patroness of mothers, grandmothers and expectant women, with great shrines such as Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupre in Quebec. She is honoured with Joachim as grandmother of Jesus.
know: Known only from Tradition, not from the Bible.
By Tradition the mother of the Virgin Mary and grandmother of Jesus.
Shares the feast of July 26 with St Joachim.

name: Jephthah's daughter
summary: Jephthah's only child, who came out with timbrels and dances to meet her victorious father and became the subject of his vow. She asked for two months to mourn her virginity on the mountains with her companions; afterward her father 'did to her according to his vow', and the daughters of Israel lamented her four days each year.
catholic: Her obedience and the annual lament of Israel's daughters have moved many Christian writers; some later interpreters argued she was dedicated to perpetual virginity rather than sacrificed, though the text is commonly read as a sacrifice. Either way, the Church reads her story as a condemnation of rash vows and of any 'offering' of innocent human life.
know: Jephthah's only child (Jdg 11:34).
Mourned her virginity two months (Jdg 11:37-38).
Israel's daughters lamented her yearly (Jdg 11:40).
Unnamed in Scripture.

name: Joachim
summary: Scripture does not name the Virgin Mary's parents. Tradition, beginning with the second-century Protoevangelium of James, names her father Joachim, a devout and prosperous man who with his wife Anne prayed long for a child.
catholic: Tradition holds that Joachim and Anne received Mary as the answer to their prayers and presented her in the Temple (commemorated on November 21). The Church honours them together as the grandparents of Jesus, and Pope Francis instituted (2021) the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly on the fourth Sunday of July, close to their feast. Their story is not Scripture, but the liturgy honours them as the parents through whom God prepared the Immaculate Mother of his Son.
know: Known only from Tradition (Protoevangelium of James), not from the Bible.
Husband of St Anne and, by Tradition, father of the Virgin Mary.
Shares the feast of July 26 with St Anne.

name: Job's wife
summary: Job's unnamed wife, who in his affliction told him, 'Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die.' Job rebuked her: 'Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?'
catholic: Her words are often read as the voice of temptation in suffering (St Augustine called her the devil's helper), though later writers have also pointed out that she too had lost all ten children. Job's reply is a classic expression of trusting acceptance of God's will.
know: Unnamed in Scripture.
Urged Job to curse God (Job 2:9).
Mentioned again in Job 19:17.

name: Mother of the seven Maccabean brothers
summary: The mother who watched her seven sons tortured and killed in one day under Antiochus IV for refusing to eat pork, encouraging each of them in their ancestral language with faith in the Creator who would give back their breath and life. After urging the youngest not to accept the king's offer, she herself died last.
catholic: 1 and 2 Maccabees are deuterocanonical books, received in the Church's canon (Rome 382, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Florence, and defined at Trent in 1546) though not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Old Testament. Her words are among Scripture's clearest statements of creation from nothing — God made all things 'not of things that were' (2 Macc 7:28; cited in CCC 297) — and of hope in bodily resurrection (2 Macc 7:22-23, 29). The Church honors her and her sons as the 'Holy Maccabees', the only Old Testament martyrs once kept on the universal Roman calendar (August 1); the Roman Martyrology still commemorates them on that day. Later tradition gives her names such as Solomonia (East) or Hannah (Jewish legend).
know: Saw seven sons die in one day (2 Macc 7:20).
Taught creation 'not of things that were' (2 Macc 7:28).
Hoped to 'receive you again with your brothers' (2 Macc 7:29).
Feast with her sons: August 1.

name: Peter's mother-in-law
summary: Simon Peter's mother-in-law lay sick with a fever in the house at Capernaum; Jesus took her by the hand, the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
catholic: Her immediate service after healing is read as a model of the grace that frees us for service. The episode also shows that Peter was married.
know: Unnamed in Scripture.
Healed in Peter's house at Capernaum (Mk 1:29-31).
Shows that Peter was married.

name: Seven Maccabean brothers
summary: Seven brothers arrested with their mother and tortured one after another before Antiochus IV for refusing swine's flesh. Each died professing faith: 'the King of the world will raise us who have died for his laws up to an everlasting renewal of life' (2 Macc 7:9).
catholic: 1 and 2 Maccabees are deuterocanonical books, received in the Church's canon (Rome 382, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Florence, and defined at Trent in 1546) though not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Old Testament. The brothers' confessions are a high point of Old Testament faith in the resurrection of the body (2 Macc 7:9, 11, 14, 23), a step in the progressive revelation of the resurrection the Catechism describes (CCC 992). The youngest's offering of his life to 'bring to an end the wrath of the Almighty' on his nation (2 Macc 7:37-38) anticipates vicarious, redemptive suffering. Honored as the 'Holy Maccabees' on August 1; tradition held their relics at Antioch, and later in Rome at San Pietro in Vincoli.
know: Group entry for the seven sons.
Hope of resurrection (2 Macc 7:9-14).
Hebrews 11:35 likely alludes to them.
Feast: August 1 (Holy Maccabees).

name: Son of Shelomith (the blasphemer)
summary: Son of an Israelite mother, Shelomith, and an Egyptian father, who cursed the Name of the LORD during a fight in the camp. He was held until the LORD's will was known, then stoned outside the camp, and the law against blasphemy was given.
catholic: The episode underlies the Second Commandment's teaching on reverence for God's name, which the Catechism treats under the commandment 'You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain' (CCC 2142).
know: Unnamed; son of Shelomith and an Egyptian (Lev 24:10).
Blasphemed the Name (Lev 24:11).
Occasion of the law in Lev 24:15-16.

name: The Levite of Judges 19
summary: Levite living in the remote hill country of Ephraim whose concubine left him for her father's house in Bethlehem. Returning with her, he lodged in Gibeah of Benjamin, where the men of the town abused her through the night until she died. He cut her body into twelve pieces and sent them through Israel, provoking war against Benjamin.
catholic: The story shows the moral collapse of an Israel without a king (Jdg 19:1; 21:25). The Church reads it as an indictment of violence against women and as preparing for God's gift of a righteous king, ultimately Christ.
know: Levite from the hill country of Ephraim (Jdg 19:1).
Lodged at Gibeah (Jdg 19:15-21).
Sent his concubine's body through Israel (Jdg 19:29).
Unnamed in Scripture.

name: The Levite's concubine
summary: Woman of Bethlehem in Judah, concubine of the Levite of Judges 19, who was given over to the men of Gibeah, abused through the night, and found dead at the door at dawn. Her death led to the war against Benjamin.
catholic: Her story, one of the darkest in Scripture, is read as a lament over human cruelty and the failure of protectors; Hosea recalls 'the days of Gibeah' as a byword for corruption (Hos 9:9; 10:9).
know: From Bethlehem in Judah (Jdg 19:1).
Abused and killed at Gibeah (Jdg 19:25-28).
Unnamed in Scripture.

name: Wife of Manoah (mother of Samson)
summary: Barren Danite woman to whom the angel of the LORD appeared, announcing that she would bear a son who would be a Nazirite to God from the womb and begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. She was to drink no wine and eat nothing unclean.
catholic: Her story stands in the line of barren mothers whose sons are gifts of God - Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth - and so prepares for the annunciation to Mary. Her calm faith ('if the LORD were pleased to kill us, he wouldn't have received a burnt offering', Jdg 13:23) contrasts with Manoah's fear.
know: Barren until the angel's visit (Jdg 13:2-3).
Told to abstain from wine and unclean food (Jdg 13:4).
Unnamed in Scripture.
Mother of Samson.
